These things we build create the "Ordinary Mind", which surrounds the Wisdom Mind. The Ordinary Mind contains all of our conscious thoughts and feelings, our knowledge, including our sense of "Self" (our name, personal history, where we went to school, whether we're a father, mother, brother, sister, etc, what we do for a living, our likes and dislikes, in short, everything we think of when we refer to ourselves).

We have been taught since childhood that this "Self" is who we are. In reality, this idea of "Self" is just an illusion. We cling to this idea of "Self" because we want to believe in something solid, something concrete. As people, we naturally want to build a framework of ideas and beliefs that we can hang our reality on. The Ordinary Mind wants to relate everything we see and feel in the world to a structure which makes us feel comfortable. Left to its own devices, the Ordinary Mind shies away from the formlessness of the Wisdom Mind. It becomes fearful of losing itself in the vast expanse, the "emptiness", which is love itself.

The reality, the truth, is that this structure, this framework, is not natural; it is of our own creation, and it covers the true reality, that of the Wisdom Mind. By stilling these thoughts, our minds have the ability to simply remain in stillness.

By quieting our mind, the thoughts, concerns, worries, and ideas of our Ordinary Mind are dissolved, revealing our Wisdom Mind. As the thoughts of the Ordinary Mind dissolve, the clouds of uncertainty dissipate and the sky clears, allowing our Wisdom Mind to shine forth.

Only by quieting the thoughts of our Ordinary Mind can we unveil the vast power that is our Wisdom Mind. The Ordinary Mind is like a curtain which is covering our Wisdom Mind. By quieting our thoughts, the curtain is drawn back and our Wisdom Mind is revealed. From that source a bright light shines forth, a light full of love and understanding, of peace and serenity.

That light is the center of your being, the core of human consciousness. That light is within you right now. It is not something new which you need to seek for, because you already have it. All that you need is inside of you. All the components to create, grow, and nurture the perfect, loving soul are within you already. Like a seed it lies in the soil, ready to blossom given the correct tending. It does require tending, though, through contemplation, understanding, meditation, good thoughts, and good deeds.

To be awakened to the nature of the Wisdom Mind is to awakened to the nature of God. The Wisdom Mind, once revealed, is the source of all divinity. God is within us. We have only to see it. When I our class was introduced to probability and statistics back in grade-school I immediately hated the subject. Not so much because I thought it was difficult, but because it just didn't seem right to me. When I was taught the Pythagorean theorem earlier on, I could find other things I could do with it; mainly, I saw it as a way to measure the distance between two points, and I could use it even in three dimensional space without having to be explicitly told how to use it. I couldn't do anything like this with anything I was taught about probability in class, and a had a feeling that there were better ways to handle the problems I was shown how to solve.

So here's the type of thing I was shown. Let's say I want to draw the winning ticket out of a hat with 20 tickets. If I pull out one ticket, I have a 1/20 chance, if I didn't get it, but I was given another chance, the next draw would give a 1/19 chance, then a 1/18 chance and so on. So taking all 20 tickets would give a 100% chance of getting that ticket. In contrast if I flip a coin there's a 50% chance of getting heads, but I don't get a 100% chance if I flip it twice. No matter how many times you flip the coin, the next toss always has a 50% chance of landing on heads.

Now if I know ahead of time that I'll get five tries pulling the tickets from the hat, it's easy to see even before I start that that gives me a 5/20 or 25% chance of winning. I was given no such guideline for the coin tosses though. This was before the Internet was readily available, and nobody I asked could explain how to come up with a solution with any confidence. Things like this annoy me. I could just flip a coin repeatedly and average the results, but as far as I was concerned that wasn't a mathematical solution. There was some fundamental logic to this that I was missing.

Eventually it occurred to me to look at all the possible outcomes that I could get after flipping the coin twice. That meant I could get two heads, two tails, or one heads and one tails. I felt like I was on the right track, but I had some reservations. For those who were taught how to handle this type of problem, it may not stand out. But these things seemed counterintuitive to me.

When drawing your first ticket you have a 1/20 chance, and if that fails but you're given one more try you have a 1/19 chance. Why is this so different from the 1/10 probability of success you'd predict knowing ahead of time that you'd get two tries? You know if you add one and one you'll get two. If you have one thing you know you'll have two if you add one more. And looking back after adding 1+1 doesn't change anything. Probabilities don't share this convenience. As far as I was concerned they didn't work like normal mathematics. Yet I was convinced there was an underlying logic hidden by my preconceptions.

So what accounts for the difference between the 1/10 and 1/19 confidence in winning even though the rules haven't changed? You're dealing with different information. Once you've finished the game you'll know if you've won or lost with 100% certainty. Before drawing you have less information to deal with. You don't know if you'll win on the first or second try, or not at all. After the first draw you'll know whether you won on the first try, this tells you more about the next try.

So maybe the coin toss wasn't as different a problem from the ticket drawing as I'd been lead to believe. If you look at the tickets you've drawn they tell you a little bit about the remaining tickets, but the coin tosses don't. Other than that their probabilities should work the same way. The first toss gives me a 50% chance of getting heads, but once I've flipped it and seen the result I'll have a better idea of whether I'll get two in a row from my next toss. Marking 0 for tails, and 1 for heads the possibilities for the first toss are 0 and 1. If I only look at the second toss it's could still be 0 or 1. But looking at the possibilities together ahead of time allows: 00, 01, 10, or 11. So does the order matter? Yes, because of the probability of the second toss. The chances of getting heads on the first try are 50%. If I flip once and see tails, the chances of getting two in a row with the next flip are 0%, but if I got heads the probability will be 50%. So not only should I predict a 25% chance because of the four possible outcomes (00, 01, 10, 11), but the prediction of the next probability should follow some rules. There's a 50% chance of getting a 50% chance on the second try. So the possible paths to take are:

 Before the first toss it's possible to get

| 0 | | 1 |
|from which you can get | |from which you can get |
| ____ ____ | | ____ ____ |
| | | | | | or | | | | | |
| |00| or |01| | | |10| or |11| |
| |__| |__| | | |__| |__| |
|_______________________| |_______________________|

Now there is a logic which makes everything fit into its proper place. I was satisfied with this reasoning and didn't bother testing the results with an actual coin. You flip a coin up to n times hoping to get two heads in a row somewhere before the end. When you get two heads in a row you win and the game is over. This is equivalent to getting at least two heads in a row after flipping the coin n times.

Probability of winning on your first two flips: 1/4

Probability of winning on your third flip: This is a little more tricky. To win on the third toss you have to get heads on the second and third flips; but the probability is less than 1/4, because if you got heads on the first and second flips you will have already won before the third one (ending the game). So this only happens if the first one lands on tails (50% probability) and the next two land on heads (25% probability). 50% of 25% is 1/8.

Probability of winning by the third flip: The sum of the probability of winning on the second flip and the probability of winning on the third flip: 25% + 12.5% = 37.5% (3/8)

7: 0000011 0001011 0010011 0100011 0101011 1000011 1001011 1010011 8 ways

Let's see if we can find a pattern... The number of ways we could win on each toss goes: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8... That looks vaguely familiar. Where have I seen that? Holy shit! It's the Fibonacci sequence! Why is this following the Fibonacci sequence and will it continue to follow this pattern?

We can't have a 1 to the left of another 1 before our two heads in a row (or else we would have won before), but there can either be a 1 or a zero to the left of each zero. So for every way of winning starting with one at the last step, we have to start with a zero at the next step; but for every pattern starting with 0 at the last step, it could start with 0 or 1 at the next step. So if we break it into strings starting with 1, and strings starting with 0, those starting with zero will be equal to all the strings from the last step, and those starting with 1 will be equal to all the strings starting with 0 from the last step, like so:

3: 011 1 way starting with 0
4: 0011 1011 2 ways: 1 starting with 0 & 1 starting with 1
5: 00011 01011 10011 3 ways: 2 starting with 0 & 1 starting with 1
6: 000011 001011 010011 100011 101011 5 ways: 3 starting with 0 & 2 starting with 1
7: 0000011 0001011 0010011 0100011 0101011 1000011 1001011 1010011 8 ways: 5 starting with 0 & 3 starting with 1

So it will continue to follow the pattern of Fibonacci numbers. The probability of winning on the nth toss is simply the Fibonacci number for that toss over 2n. The probability of winning by that toss is the sum of the probability of winning for each toss made.
